_about: Recipe distance (Here / Nearby / Anywhere) per market. Here = the market's own kitchen plus what arrived and stayed (everyday in homes or high streets, not only within one community). Nearby = neighbours (hand-drawn: kitchens a cook there would call next door) plus family (kitchens joined by a documented dish-level exchange, vetted against sources 2026-09-28). Anywhere = every kitchen not in Here or Nearby. The climate band in markets.json decides seasons only, never cooking. `care: true` means the link is real but the proof must be worded exactly as `proof` says. `legends` are popular stories historians reject: the engine must never state them as fact. A new market needs three hand-written entries: here, neighbours, family.

family.proof: Feijoada descends from Portuguese pork-and-bean stews; black beans are the Brazilian substitution.
Vindaloo takes its name and method from Portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos, with palm vinegar for wine.
Macanese cooking is a Portuguese, Cantonese and Southeast Asian fusion from the 16th century on, carrying dishes like bacalhau and cabidela.
Kasutera grew from the pão de ló Portuguese missionaries brought to Nagasaki; tempura's batter frying arrived through the same Nanban trade.
Foi thong comes from Portuguese fios de ovos, thong yip from trouxas de ovos.
The piri-piri chilli and sauce came to Portugal from Portuguese Mozambique.
The Portuguese-Eurasian community of Malacca cooks curry debal, a vinegar-soured Christmas curry.
Chocolate reached the Spanish court from Mexico in the 16th century and was sweetened and spiced in Spain; modern mole carries Old World spices, nuts and bread.
Philippine empanadas and leche flan descend from their Spanish originals; adobo took the Spanish name for a native vinegar braise.
Ropa vieja came to Cuba from Spain via Canary Islanders and is recorded there by 1857.
Argentina's regional empanadas descend from the Iberian empanada recorded in the Cantigas and the Llibre del Coch.
Spanish-borne citrus and onion reshaped a pre-Hispanic raw-fish dish into ceviche.

naturalised.proof: Couscous came to France with the pieds-noirs in the 1960s and ranks among France's favourite dishes.

family.proof: Bánh mì puts French baguette and pâté into a Saigon sandwich.
Louisiana gumbo is built on a French roux, cooked darker.
Tourtière is named for the French tourtière pie dish.
Provençal pistou comes from Genoese pesto, without the pine nuts.
Fainá is Genoese farinata, brought by Ligurian immigrants; milanesa is cotoletta alla milanese.
Baasto, spaghetti with suugo suqaar, became a staple under Italian rule.
Pasta al sugo e berbere joins Italian pasta and tomato to Eritrean spice.
Macaroni dishes (macaroona) came with Italian rule.

naturalised.proof: The döner sandwich was popularised in West Berlin from the early 1970s (Berlin popularised it; it did not invent it).
Spaghettieis was created in Mannheim in 1969 by Dario Fontanella of an Italian gelato family.

family.proof: German settlers brought kuchen to southern Chile in the 19th century.
Palatine German immigrants brought the soft pretzel to Pennsylvania.
Vienna's first coffeehouse was opened by the Armenian Johannes Diodato, who brought coffee from Ottoman lands; strudel probably descends from Ottoman layered pastry.

naturalised.proof: The rijsttafel came with repatriates from the Indies and is on the Dutch intangible heritage register; nasi and saté are everyday Dutch food.
Pom became popular in the Netherlands through Surinamese migration.

family.proof: Coleslaw (koolsla) and cookies (koekjes) came from New Netherland.
The koeksister is probably from Dutch koek, mixed with Cape Malay and Indonesian influence.
Poulet moambe was the Congolese dish Belgian colonials cooked most, and is served today in Brussels' Matonge.
The Belgian waffle was introduced to Americans at the 1962 and 1964 World's Fairs, based on the Brussels waffle.

naturalised.proof: Kedgeree is khichri with fish, common in 19th-century British cookbooks; mulligatawny is Tamil milagu-thanni.
Balti was created in Birmingham around 1975.
Sylheti cooks run most of Britain's 'Indian' restaurants.

family.proof: The Jamaican patty is usually described as a descendant of the British pasty, remade with scotch bonnet.
Hong Kong-style milk tea adapted British milk tea, with evaporated milk and a cloth strainer.
Marmalade takes its name from Portuguese marmelada, a quince paste imported into England from the 15th century.
Corned beef and cabbage is Irish-American: New York immigrants put corned brisket in place of the bacon in bacon and cabbage.

naturalised.proof: Cajsa Warg's cookbook (1765 edition) gives a dolma and suggests cabbage leaves in place of vine leaves.

family.proof: Swedish punsch is built on Batavia arrack, first shipped to Gothenburg by the Swedish East India Company in 1733.

legends: Feijoada was made by enslaved people from pork scraps.
Catherine de' Medici brought Italian cooking to France.
The croissant was invented in Vienna to celebrate the 1683 siege.
Kolschitzky opened Vienna's first coffeehouse with beans the Turks left behind.
Wiener Schnitzel came from Milan via Radetzky.
Worcestershire sauce came from a recipe Lord Sandys brought back from Bengal.
Fish and chips' fried fish was brought by Portuguese Jews (a popular claim historians dispute).
Charles XII's soldiers brought kåldolmar back from Turkey.
Dulce de leche was invented in 1829 during the Rosas-Lavalle meeting.
Chicken tikka masala was invented in Glasgow (only ever 'claimed by' Glasgow).
Mole was invented by the nuns of a Puebla convent.
